== Biography ==
{{Ireland Native}}

'''James Glasgow''' was born about 1801 in County Antrim, Ireland. In the surviving 1851 census he was a fifty-year-old day labourer at Ballycregagh, Dunaghy, County Antrim.<ref name="Census1851">1851 Census of Ireland, County Antrim, Dunaghy parish, Ballycraigargh, household 29, James Glasgow household: [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QSQ-G94X-YD22 living household, image 251] and [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-L94X-Y621 continuation and mortality return, image 252].</ref>

James and [[Hamilton-25516|Peggy Hamilton]] were both recorded as having married in 1848. Peggy's unmarried sisters [[Hamilton-44032|Nancy Hamilton]] and [[Hamilton-44033|Jane Hamilton]] lived with them. The mortality portion of the return names Peggy's parents as [[Hamilton-44031|Robert Hamilton]], a linen weaver, and [[Unknown-764457|Cathrin Hamilton]], both of whom died in spring 1848.<ref name="Census1851" />

The same return identifies James's children:

An 1847 Ballymena Workhouse admission group records [[Unknown-764460|Mary Glasgow]], aged 34, married and deserted, at Glenleslie with Margaret, Boyd, William James and Mary Jane Glasgow. Their names, ages and locality correspond closely to four of James's children in 1851.<ref name="Workhouse1847">[https://www.billmacafee.com/otherrecords/ballymenaworkhouse.pdf William Macafee, "Admissions to Ballymena Workhouse: 13th May to 8th July 1847"], registrations 4406–4410, Mary, Boyd, William James, Mary Jane and Margaret Glasgow of Glenleslie (accessed 13 August 2026).</ref>


=== Glenleslie parentage and daughter Ann ===

The 1851 census of [[Glasgow-1022|John Glasgow]] at Glenleslie records [[Glasgow-3168|Ann Glasgow]], aged eighteen, as his granddaughter.<ref name="Glenleslie1851">[https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/census-record/#census_year=1851&surname__icontains=Glasgow&county=Antrim&limit=30&id=31214 1851 Census of Ireland], Glenleslie household 21, John Glasgow household.</ref> Ann Jane Glasgow married Patrick Russell on 24 November 1869. The original register describes her as a thirty-three-year-old spinster of Kildowney and names her father as James Glasgow, weaver.<ref name="AnnRussell1869">General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage register, Patrick Russell and Ann Jane Glasgow, 24 November 1869, Ballymena registration district; [https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1869/11434/8200208.pdf original register image].</ref>

The bride is the strongest and only located identity for John's census granddaughter: her age is close, Kildowney and Glenleslie are both in Dunaghy parish, and this James's independently documented family was at Glenleslie in 1847. The combined records identify Ann as James's daughter and James as a son of John Glasgow. No source identifies Ann's mother; neither Mary nor Peggy is attached to her.== Research Notes ==

=== Individual father review, 22 October 2026 ===

The existing father [[Glasgow-1022]] is assessed at 98% (proved). The 1851 Glenleslie census calls Ann John’s granddaughter; her 1869 marriage names father James, weaver. James-2981’s 1847 Glenleslie family and 1851 neighbouring Dunaghy household identify the specific local James. The combined generation and household records support James as John’s son with confidence.

Confident inferred father98%; John’s own father and both unknown mothers are not proved by the granddaughter chain. The 1825 junior suffix alone is not a son clause.

Next useful test: Use the 1847/1851 household records to resolve the remaining child and maternal questions.

Source basis already held: [https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-2981 WikiTree profile export for Glasgow-2981]. No new original inspected; no new father attached.



The 1851 return records James and Peggy's marriage year as 1848. This means Peggy should not be treated as the proved mother of children born between about 1831 and 1846, but it does not make earlier biological maternity impossible. Mary of the 1847 workhouse group is the strongest identified candidate for James's earlier wife and the older children's mother, but no inspected marriage or other record explicitly names James as Mary's husband. Until a better-supported mother can be attached, Peggy should remain attached to those children with uncertain confidence.

The workhouse transcription says that its Mary Jane died on 27 November 1847, while the 1851 return records an eleven-year-old Mary Jane living with James. This could reflect a transcription or return error, or two same-named children, and should not be resolved without the original records.

The [https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/search-results/#census_year=1851&surname__icontains=Glasgow&county=Antrim&parish__icontains=Dunaghy&townland__icontains=Ballycre&house_number=29&limit=30 National Archives of Ireland household link] cited on the profile is preserved. The public detailed transcription supplies the accessible household data used here.

James's parents have not been identified. His location places him in the wider Dunaghy Glasgow population, but no record calls him a son of [[Glasgow-1022|John Glasgow]], [[Glasgow-1367|Robert Glasgow]], [[Glasgow-3904|Alexander Glasgow]], or either 1825 Ballybogy tithe occupier. [[Glasgow-1702]] and [[Glasgow-1573]] remain similar-name profiles, not proved duplicates.
* Death index entry: James Glasgow, 24 April 1865, aged 66, Cookstown district, D/1865/99/1009/1/329. [https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk/search/death GRONI death index].

== Research Notes ==
A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Belfast Juvenile Society secretary, 1830–1831. James Glasgow and Walter Moffat are named secretaries announcing the Belfast Juvenile Society’s sixth annual meeting at Rev. Dr Cooke’s May Street meeting-house on Monday 15 November 1830. In March 1831 Rev. Walter Moffatt and Mr James Glasgow attended a Knockbracken meeting as the Society’s deputation; Rev. Thomas Houston chaired it.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 12 November 1830, p.2, Belfast Juvenile Society sixth annual meeting announcement; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390573239/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 4 March 1831, p.4, Belfast Juvenile Society, Knockbracken meeting; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390543442/ record].</ref> The repeated society and associates support one society account. The same Walter Moffat appears in the 1828 Institution report, making [[Glasgow-1780]] a compatible student/ministry-network candidate; this does not prove that the society secretary is the college student. The newspaper does not call James the president, chair or minister. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Belfast tobacco seller, 1822–23. James Glasgow offered leaf tobacco in three Belfast advertisements in 1822–23. The August 1822 notice directs buyers to him at James M’Master’s; the May 1823 notice locates samples at M’Master’s North Street premises.<ref>The Irishman, 15 March 1822, p. 2, tobacco advertisement dated 9 March; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/61259036/ record]; The Irishman, 23 August 1822, p. 3, tobacco advertisement dated 20 August; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/61260054/ record]; The Irishman, 30 May 1823, p. 3, tobacco advertisement dated 27 May; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/61261904/ record].</ref> Repeated name, trade and contact support a consolidated seller account. M’Master’s premises are a commercial contact, not a proved home or owned property. No age, family or link to William Glasgow the grocer is stated. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Belfast tobacco seller, 1822–23. An auction notice describes the large shop and stores at No.32 Rosemary Street, Belfast, as formerly occupied by Mr James Glasgow. The lease interest was offered for sale on 1 April 1828; the notice dated 21 March gives 34 years unexpired from 1 November next and £30 late Irish currency yearly rent.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 1 April 1828, p.3, auction of shop and stores, No.32 Rosemary Street; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390544933/ record].</ref> Former occupancy is explicit; ownership, trade and residence are not. The surname is certain, but identity with the 1822–23 tobacco seller, William the grocer or another James remains unproved. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, Kilrea procession case, 1835–1836. James Glasgow was among the men indicted after a procession and alleged riot at Kilrea on 13 July 1835. The procession count was set aside under the amnesty; the trial proceeded on the riot charge and the jury immediately acquitted the prisoners.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 25 March 1836, p.1, Kilrea Orangemen, indictment and acquittal; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390543681/ record].</ref> The court report establishes an accused surname bearer and acquittal, not a conviction, residence, occupation or kinship. Regional James Glasgow candidates remain unassigned. No connection to Alexander or Robert of Lisnagaver is supplied. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, plaintiff in Dublin Exchequer, 1820. James Glasgow was plaintiff against Maxwell Lepper and Clotworthy Dobbin in a Court of Exchequer report headed Dublin, 22 June 1820. The defendants’ motion to rescind the contempt process was refused with costs and liberty for the plaintiff to continue process.<ref>The Irishman, 30 June 1820, p. 2, Court of Exchequer, Dublin, 22 June; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/61258711/ record].</ref> The report gives a procedural decision, not final judgment on the dispute, and no age, occupation, residence or relatives for James. George Frederick Moulds is named as plaintiff’s agent. Identity with the later Belfast tobacco seller or any candidate is unproved. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, plaintiff in Dublin Exchequer, 1820. A separate report lists James Glasgow on the petty jury for Friday 1 August 1828. He is a juror, not one of the accused in the following riot-and-assault report.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 5 August 1828, p.4, petty jury, Friday 1 August; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390549197/ record].</ref> The name is James Glasgow, not the automated index’s combined William James Glasgow. No residence, occupation or kin is stated. This remains an unassigned legal occurrence; identity with the 1820 Exchequer plaintiff is unproved. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, plaintiff in Dublin Exchequer, 1820. A report in the Freeman’s Journal and Daily Commercial Advertiser states that the parties in cause and cross-cause included Robert Thompson of Newry, the Rev. Mr Walsh of Ballymena, and Mr Barbour of Lisburn; it then says “The following were the Jury” and lists James Glasgow.<ref>Freeman's Journal and Daily Commercial Advertiser, 3 November 1823, p. 3, trial report and jury list; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/1050060364/ record].</ref> The original page confirms James Glasgow’s jury role in this reported trial. The newspaper issue is from Dublin, but the inspected passage does not show a court heading or venue. Newry, Ballymena and Lisburn describe other named parties, not the juror. The occurrence is compatible with, but not proved to be the same person as, the James Glasgow on the 1828 Belfast petty jury; identity with the 1820 Exchequer plaintiff is also unproved. The identification remains uncertain.
